articles.title: What a zone is
articles.summary: A zone is a group of pixels that gets one finish: which pixels it covers and what look they get. Add Zone, then pick a colour off the car or pick a part; a zone can also be locked to layers.
articles.what: Your paint is a flat picture of the whole car. A zone points at part of it, by colour, by layer, by a drawn shape or by a named car part, and gives that part a finish: a base material such as gloss, matte, satin, chrome, candy, pearl or metallic, or a complete special look. A zone can also carry a colour setting, a pattern on top, spec patterns that change shine and roughness, an optional second base blended over the first, and strength sliders. Every zone is a card in the ZONES column on the left. Click a card to open its ZONE POPOUT PANEL, where all of that is edited. A new zone does nothing until it has both a way to pick pixels and a finish.
when: You are starting out and want the one idea that everything else hangs on.
A buyer says "I changed the finish but nothing happened".
how: 1. Press + Add Zone in the ZONES column.
2. Click the new card to open its popout panel.
3. In COLOR, say which pixels it owns, for example PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click the red stripe.
4. In BASE, open Base Material and pick a finish.
5. Watch LIVE PREVIEW. Press RENDER when you are happy.

controls.effect: Adds an empty zone at the top.

controls.label: Reset All Zones
controls.effect: Resets to the default set of zones (confirmed, undoable).

controls.effect: Opens the More menu (presets, randomise, apply to all, library, templates, SHOKK files, channel PNG export).

The card shows a hint when something is missing, for example "Pick a base finish AND a color".
pitfalls: + Add Zone puts the new card at the bottom of the list, below Everything Else. Everything Else takes every pixel not claimed above it, so drag the new card above it (or press Ctrl+Up) or it gets nothing.
A zone with no colour, layer or region set covers nothing.
A zone with a colour but no finish shows your paint unchanged.

deep.heading: What every new session starts with
deep.body: Shokker opens with five zones: Zone 1 to Zone 4 are empty slots and Everything Else sits at the bottom. Zones 1 and 2 start with a colour match of plus or minus 40, Zone 3 with 35 and Zone 4 with 30. Zone 4 also starts at intensity 80, and Everything Else is a gloss base at intensity 50. Each empty slot carries a hint, such as click your PRIMARY body color, until you use it.

deep.heading: Two halves: which pixels, and what look
deep.body: A zone is only finished when it has both. Pixel choice can be a picked colour, a layer, a drawn box or lasso, or the Remaining catch-all. The look starts with Base Material, which always supplies the shine map (metal, roughness, clearcoat). Under Base Color you choose where the colour comes from: Use finish's own color, Use source paint (spec only), Use solid color, From special, or Custom gradient.

deep.heading: The sliders a zone carries
deep.body: In BASE you get Hue Shift (-180 to 180), Saturation (-100 to 100), Brightness (-100 to 200), Base Strength and Spec Strength (both 0 to 100 percent in steps of 5, starting at 100). R Metal, G Rough and B Coat each shift that channel from -127 to 127 in steps of 5. Intensity on the card runs 10 to 100 percent in tens.

deep.heading: How many zones you can really use
deep.body: The app stops you at 50 zones and warns once you reach 30. The practical ceiling is lower: about 20 zones that have their own painted area (a box, a layer or a part) before the preview or render runs out of memory. Zones that only pick a colour are cheaper. Merge zones that share one look.

deep.heading: What happens to pixels no zone touches
deep.body: Pixels that no zone claims keep your source paint and get the plain default shine: metallic 5, roughness 100, clearcoat 16, mask 255. That is why Everything Else exists. It guarantees every pixel has a deliberate finish instead of the default.

The bottom zone is the safety net that makes sure no pixel is left on the default shine.
Most the zone does nothing complaints come from a missing half: no finish, or no way to pick pixels.

faq.q: How many zones should I use?
faq.a: Two or three cover most cars: body, trim or stripes, and numbers. The app starts you with four open slots plus Everything Else on purpose.

faq.q: Is there a maximum number of zones?
faq.a: 50 is the hard stop and you get a warning at 30. The real limit is about 20 zones that each have their own painted area, because the preview and render run out of memory beyond that.

faq.q: Does a zone change my original paint file?
faq.a: No. Zones are instructions applied when you render. Your source paint is untouched, and Reset Zone or Reset All Zones puts the instructions back.

faq.q: Why does my new zone do nothing?
faq.a: A new zone has no colour, layer or box and no finish. It needs both a way to pick pixels and a Base Material. The dot on the card turns green and says Will render only when both are set.

faq.q: What is the difference between a zone and a layer?
faq.a: A layer is a piece of your PSD artwork. A zone is a finish instruction. A zone can be tied to a layer with RESTRICT TO LAYERS, but they are separate things.

faq.q: Is a zone the same as a layer?
faq.a: No. A zone is a group of pixels on the car that gets one finish; a layer is a picture inside your paint file. You can lock a zone to layers with RESTRICT TO LAYERS so it only touches those layers.

faq.q: What is a zone, is it like a layer?
faq.a: A zone is a group of pixels that gets one finish (which pixels, and what look they get); a layer is a layer from your template or PSD. They are separate, but a zone can be locked to layers with RESTRICT TO LAYERS so it only touches those layers.

mistakes.symptom: You picked a finish and the car looks identical
mistakes.cause: The zone has a finish but no colour, layer or box, so it covers no pixels.
mistakes.fix: Open COLOR and press PICK COLOR FROM CAR, then click the area on the canvas.

mistakes.symptom: You picked a colour and nothing changes
mistakes.cause: The zone has pixels but no Base Material.
mistakes.fix: Open BASE, press Base Material and choose a finish. The card shows No finish assigned until you do.

mistakes.symptom: Preview or render fails after adding lots of zones
mistakes.cause: More than about 20 zones with their own painted area exhausts the memory the render uses for masks.
mistakes.fix: Merge zones that share a look, or drop boxes and layers you no longer need, then press F5.

protips: A zone can be seen as its coloured dot: green means Will render, orange means it has no finish or no pixels, red means its layer is missing, grey means muted or empty.
Pick Use source paint (spec only) as the Base Color when you only want a different shine. The Base Material still supplies the shine map, and your colours stay put.

articles.title: How a zone picks its pixels: colour, layer, region and part
articles.summary: A zone can find its pixels four ways: by colour, by layer, by a drawn shape, or by a named car part. You can combine them: all must match.
articles.what: By colour: pick one or several colours and a tolerance; every pixel near those colours belongs to the zone. By layer: restrict the zone to pixels on chosen PSD layers such as Numbers, Sponsors or Car Paint. By region: draw a box, a lasso shape or a brush area and the zone only affects what is inside. By part: say "the hood" or "the left side" and the helper uses the car's named parts (this is how Chat and the AI copilot aim a zone). One quick chip, Remaining, covers every pixel that no higher zone claimed. Combined rules narrow the zone: colour plus layer means that colour, but only on that layer.
when: You want "only the red parts" or "only the numbers".
A colour also appears on logos and bleeds into them.
how: 1. For a colour, use PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click it on the canvas.
2. For a layer, tick it under RESTRICT TO LAYERS.
3. For a shape, use Draw box or Lasso under APPLY AREA.
4. Combine them if the colour shows in too many places.

deep.heading: The four pickers narrow each other
deep.body: Colour, layer, drawn area and the Exclude and Include brushes all stack as AND. A pixel must pass every test you have set. The zone first takes the drawn box or lasso, multiplies it by the colour match, applies the brushes, then limits it to the ticked layers. Adding a rule can only shrink a zone, never grow it.

deep.heading: Several colours add up instead
deep.body: Each further click with PICK COLOR FROM CAR adds another colour chip. The chips work as OR: a pixel belongs to the zone if it is close to any one of them, and it takes the strongest match. Every chip has its own Exact to Loose slider, shown as plus or minus a number, so a stripe colour can be tight while the body colour is loose.

deep.heading: How close is close enough
deep.body: Closeness is measured on a 0 to 255 scale, but not equally in every colour: green differences count most (weight 0.59), red next (0.30), blue least (0.11). A pixel at the exact picked colour gets full strength, and strength falls in a straight line to nothing at the tolerance. With Hard Edge on, every pixel with any match at all becomes fully owned. With Hard Edge off, matches below about 15 percent strength fade out.

deep.heading: With a layer ticked, the colour is read from that layer
deep.body: If the zone is restricted to a layer, the colour match is made on that layer's own pixels, not on the finished picture with everything stacked on top. This fixes semi-transparent art, where the visible colour is a blend and does not match the layer's real colour. Pick the colour while that layer is visible and you get the match you expect.

deep.heading: Quick chips and the part route
deep.body: Remaining is the only catch-all chip: it takes whatever no other zone measured. Naming a part like the hood is a Chat and Shokker AI route. It turns the name into an exact mask of that panel, optionally a portion such as the rear half. Plain Pro uses colour, layer, box and lasso.

examples.title: Yellow on the body only, not on the logo
examples.goal: Give the yellow body panels a pearl finish and leave the yellow logo alone.
examples.result: Only yellow that sits on the body layer is caught. The yellow in the logo layer keeps its original look.

examples.title: Number fill without the outline
examples.goal: Chrome only the dark fill of the numbers, keeping the white and black outlines.
examples.result: A tight match of about 10 to 16 on the numbers layer takes the fill and leaves both strokes. Dark fills are often close to a black stroke, so keep it tight.

examples.title: Two stripe shades in one zone
examples.goal: One finish for a red stripe that has a darker red edge.

settings.PICK COLOR FROM CAR: click the red, then click the darker red
settings.Color Match sliders: 40 for the main red, 25 for the dark edge

examples.result: Both shades belong to one zone and use one finish, each with its own reach.

combos.why: Tolerance decides how wide each colour chip reaches, which is the main reason a colour pick catches too much or too little.
A layer is the exact way to stop a colour bleeding into logos that share the colour.
A box or lasso is the way to split two panels that are the same colour on the flat sheet.

faq.q: Can I mix colour and layer rules?
faq.a: Yes. They combine as AND, so colour plus layer means that colour, but only on that layer.

faq.q: Do I have to pick a colour at all?
faq.a: No. A zone can be only a layer (MAKE ZONE on the layer card), only a box or lasso, or the Remaining catch-all.

faq.q: How do I add a second colour to the same zone?
faq.a: Press PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click another colour. Each click adds a chip. Pressing Set in the Color tool bar replaces everything with one colour instead.

faq.q: Why does a colour I picked catch the edge of other colours too?
faq.a: Edge pixels are blends of two colours, so they land inside your tolerance. Lower that chip's Color Match slider or restrict the zone to a layer.

faq.q: Is the left or right side of the car the left or right of the sheet?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Parts are named for the car, and one side may sit upside down on the flat sheet.

mistakes.symptom: A numbers zone also changes sponsor logos
mistakes.cause: The same colour exists on both and the zone only has a colour rule.
mistakes.fix: Tick the Numbers layer under RESTRICT TO LAYERS so the zone cannot reach other art.

mistakes.symptom: A colour zone turns into a ragged speckle
mistakes.cause: The tolerance is too tight for a shaded or anti-aliased area.
mistakes.fix: Slide that chip toward Loose in steps of about 10 and watch the overlay until the area fills in.

mistakes.symptom: Adding a box made the zone cover less than before
mistakes.cause: Rules combine as AND, so a box can only shrink a colour zone.
mistakes.fix: Clear the box, or draw it large enough to include everything you want.

protips: Pick the colour while the layer you restrict to is visible. The match is made on that layer's own pixels, so a picture of the stacked result can mislead you.
Give every chip its own reach. A body colour can be loose enough to cover shading while a stripe next to it stays tight.

articles.title: Zone priority: the top zone wins
articles.summary: The zone higher in the list wins a pixel, so reorder zones (drag one up, or Ctrl+Up) to change who wins. A layer-tied zone gets visible ownership only where its layer shows; pixels no zone claims go to Everything Else.
articles.what: The first zone in the list has the highest priority. A lower zone only gets the pixels the zones above it did not claim. So a new zone that must show on pixels another zone already owns has to sit above it. Drag the handle on a zone card to reorder, or press Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down with the zone selected. The catch-all zone, Everything Else, belongs at the bottom. A zone you add with + Add Zone lands below it, so move it up. If a zone "does nothing", the usual reason is that a zone above it already claims those pixels.
when: A zone is not showing.
Two zones overlap and the wrong one wins.
how: 1. Look at the ZONES list: top is highest priority.
2. Drag the zone you want to win above the other one, or select it and press Ctrl+Up.
3. Watch the preview update.
4. Keep Everything Else at the bottom, and drag any zone you just added above it.

controls.label: Zone order (drag handle and priority)
controls.default: + Add Zone puts it at the bottom; Chat and the AI copilot put new zones at the top
controls.effect: Top zone wins where two zones select the same pixels.

tips: Alt+1 to Alt+9 select a zone; Up and Down arrows move the selection through the list.
Specific zones (numbers, stripes) go above general ones (body).
pitfalls: "Remaining" zones belong at the bottom. Higher zones win overlaps.
Muting a zone with the eye icon is a quick test for "is something above it?".

deep.heading: First come, first served
deep.body: Shokker walks down the list from the top. Each zone measures what it can catch, and pixels already taken by zones above are not given again. Zone 1 has first pick, then Zone 2, and so on. The order of the list is the priority setting, and there is no number to type. One exception: a zone that picks by colour or layer, has no box or lasso, and has green Include brush marks wins those marked pixels even over zones above it.

deep.heading: Remaining is measured last
deep.body: A Remaining zone such as Everything Else is not worked out in its list position. The render first measures every colour, layer and area zone, then gives Remaining whatever none of them caught. So Remaining can never take pixels from a zone below it. Keep it at the bottom anyway: that is where it reads naturally.

deep.heading: Layer zones are decided by what you can see
deep.body: A zone tied to a layer owns the pixels where that layer is really visible: at least half opaque after layer opacity, and not covered by artwork above it. Artwork on top of a body layer is therefore never claimed by the body zone. List order still settles overlaps between zones that cover the same pixels.

deep.heading: Where a new zone lands
deep.body: + Add Zone puts the new card at the bottom of the list, below Everything Else, selects it and scrolls down to it. Presets and Chat are different: Chat places new zones at the top. If a new zone must beat existing ones, move it up yourself.

deep.heading: Ways to move and find zones
deep.body: Drag the three-line handle on a card. Or select a zone and press Ctrl+Up or Ctrl+Down to move it one place. Up and Down arrows only move the selection. Alt+1 to Alt+9 jump straight to zone 1 to 9. Every move refreshes the live preview, so you see the winner immediately.

examples.goal: The car number should be chrome but it keeps showing the body finish.

settings.Key: Ctrl+Up until it is above the body zone

examples.result: The numbers zone now has first pick of its pixels, so the chrome shows. The body zone keeps the rest.

examples.title: Stripe on top of a similar body colour
examples.goal: A red stripe sits on a dark red body and both zones catch the stripe.
examples.result: The tight stripe zone wins where the colours overlap and the looser body zone takes everything else.

examples.title: Find which zone is hiding yours
examples.goal: Your zone shows nothing and you do not know why.

settings.Step 1: Click the eye icon on each zone above yours, one at a time
settings.Step 2: Watch LIVE PREVIEW after each click
settings.Step 3: When your zone appears, drag it above that one

examples.result: The zone whose mute makes yours appear is the one holding your pixels.

combos.why: A zone above is the most common reason a zone shows nothing, so check order first.
The catch-all belongs at the bottom and never competes with the zones above.
Layer zones are decided by visibility, so art on top stays with its own zone.

faq.q: Which zone wins when two zones want the same pixel?
faq.a: The one higher in the list. The top card has the highest priority.

faq.q: Does Remaining need to be last?
faq.a: It is worked out after every other zone anyway, so it cannot steal pixels. The bottom is still the right place and the one the app expects.

faq.q: Do Chat and the AI copilot put zones at the top?
faq.a: Yes. They place new zones at the top by default, so a new look wins over older zones.

faq.q: Can I give two zones the same pixels on purpose?
faq.a: The upper one takes them. To layer a second look on the same pixels, use the zone's second base overlay or a pattern instead.

faq.q: Does the eye icon change priority?
faq.a: No. It only hides the zone from the render and preview so you can test what is underneath. Click it again to bring the zone back.

faq.q: How do I change which zone wins?
faq.a: Reorder the zones: drag the zone you want to win above the other one in the ZONES list, or select it and press Ctrl+Up.

faq.q: The top of my car looks right but the bottom is the wrong colour.
faq.a: Pixels that no zone claims go to Everything Else, so a zone covering only the top leaves the bottom to it. Widen that zone's region or box down to the rocker, or give Everything Else the finish you want, and check that no higher zone is stealing the pixels.

mistakes.symptom: A new zone does nothing because the old body zone already took everything
mistakes.cause: + Add Zone puts the new card at the bottom, so every zone above it wins.
mistakes.fix: Drag the new card above the body zone, or select it and press Ctrl+Up.

mistakes.symptom: Ctrl+Up does nothing
mistakes.cause: The zone is already at the top, or the focus is inside a text box.
mistakes.fix: Click the zone card first, not a field, then press the keys again.

mistakes.symptom: You reordered but the preview looks the same
mistakes.cause: The two zones cover different pixels, so order made no difference there.
mistakes.fix: Order only matters where zones overlap. Mute one zone to see which pixels they share.

protips: Specific zones go above general ones: numbers and stripes above the body, the body above Everything Else.
The eye icon is the quickest priority test. If a zone appears the moment you hide another, you have found the one in the way.

articles.title: Everything Else: the safety net zone
articles.summary: Everything Else is the catch-all zone at the bottom of the list. It gives a base finish to every pixel no other zone claimed; if only one part looks right, check priority and regions.
articles.what: A fresh Shokker session starts with four open zones and one Everything Else zone. Everything Else catches whatever the zones above it left alone, so nothing on the car is ever left without a finish. By default it uses a gloss base at 50 percent intensity. It works because it is last: any zone above it wins overlaps. If you move it up, it can swallow pixels meant for zones below.
when: You want the whole body to have a base shine without picking its colours.
Parts of the car you did not select look wrong or unfinished.
how: 1. Find Everything Else at the bottom of the ZONES list and click it.
2. In BASE, choose the finish you want for the leftovers.
3. Leave it at the bottom of the list.

controls.default: new zones go to the TOP via the kit
controls.effect: Makes this zone the catch-all: it gets every pixel no zone above it claims.

tips: A "Remaining" colour chip on any zone makes it a catch-all too. Use only one at the bottom.
pitfalls: If Everything Else sits above other zones, those zones can lose pixels.

deep.heading: What its factory settings mean
deep.body: Everything Else starts as the Remaining catch-all with the Gloss base at intensity 50. Gloss is a standard glossy body with metal 0, roughness 30 and clearcoat 16, described in the app as the safe default under sponsors and numbers. Intensity 50 applies the spec, paint and brightness effects at half strength, so the leftovers stay close to your original paint.

deep.heading: It is measured after everything else
deep.body: The render first measures every colour, layer and area zone. Only then does Remaining take the pixels that none of them caught. With Hard Edge on, which is the default, the catch-all has no feathered edge, so there are no halos or outlines around logos and numbers. Pixels inside lettering, such as the hole of a zero, fall to Everything Else too, unless a zone claims them.

deep.heading: Inside a layer, Remaining means what is left of that layer
deep.body: If a Remaining zone is tied to a layer, for example Numbers, it takes only what is left inside that layer after earlier zones restricted to the same layer. Earlier zones that cover the whole car do not erase it. This lets you give one zone to the number's fill and a Remaining zone to the rest of the number.

deep.heading: Without it, the default shine applies
deep.body: If you delete Everything Else, untouched pixels keep your source paint and get the plain default shine of metal 5, roughness 100, clearcoat 16. The app will let you delete it, but you lose the guarantee that every pixel is finished on purpose.

deep.heading: You can have more than one
deep.body: Any zone can be made Remaining with the Remaining chip under COLOR. A second Remaining zone only sees what the first one left, which is nothing unless it is restricted to a layer. Use a layer to split the leftovers, such as body versus sponsor art.

examples.title: Keep sponsors readable, finish everything else
examples.goal: Chrome stripes, everything else in a quiet gloss.

settings.Zone 1 > COLOR: PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the stripes

examples.result: The stripes mirror, and every other pixel, including sponsors, stays a calm gloss close to the original paint.

examples.title: Flat low-sheen car with one shiny part
examples.goal: Low sheen everywhere except the hood.
examples.result: The hood is candy and the rest gets the eggshell powder-coat shine with colours untouched.

examples.title: Different finish for the body and for what is left of the numbers
examples.goal: Give the number fill chrome and the rest of the number layer matte.
examples.result: Zone 1 takes the fill, and Zone 2 takes the outline pixels left on the Numbers layer.

combos.why: Everything Else sits last, so every zone above gets first pick.
Pairing a layer with Remaining splits a layer between two zones.
A Foundation finish with Use source paint on the catch-all changes only the shine and keeps every colour.

faq.q: Can I delete Everything Else?
faq.a: Yes, as long as one zone remains. Then untouched pixels keep your paint with the plain default shine instead of a deliberate finish.

faq.q: Why did my logo change when I only edited Everything Else?
faq.a: No zone claimed the logo, so the catch-all did. Give the logo its own zone, or keep the catch-all to Gloss with Use source paint.

faq.q: Is Everything Else the same as Remaining?
faq.a: Yes. Everything Else is a zone whose colour is set to the Remaining chip. Any zone can use the chip.

faq.q: Can I move it to the top?
faq.a: You can, and it still only gets what no other zone caught, because it is measured last. The bottom is the clearer place.

faq.q: Can Everything Else paint over a zone I set up?
faq.a: No. Zones with their own pixels are measured first and the catch-all only gets what is left. If your zone looks weak, check its Color Match and its place in the list.

faq.q: Why is the bottom of my car the wrong colour?
faq.a: Pixels that no zone claimed go to Everything Else, so a zone that only covers the top leaves the bottom to it. Widen the region of that zone down to the rocker, or give Everything Else the colour you want.

faq.q: One part looks right but the rest of the panels are dull or the wrong colour?
faq.a: Pixels no zone claimed go to Everything Else, and a higher zone wins overlaps. Widen the right zone over the other panels, or give Everything Else the finish and colour you want.

mistakes.symptom: The whole car turned chrome
mistakes.cause: Everything Else was given Chrome with a solid colour, so every unclaimed pixel changed.
mistakes.fix: Set the catch-all back to Gloss, or switch its Base Color to Use source paint (spec only).

mistakes.symptom: A thin line around numbers has a different shine
mistakes.cause: The edge pixels were claimed by neither the number zone nor the body zone, so Everything Else took them.
mistakes.fix: Raise the number zone's Color Match a little, or tie it to the Numbers layer, so it covers its own edge.

mistakes.symptom: Two catch-all zones and the second one shows nothing
mistakes.cause: The first Remaining zone already took every leftover pixel.
mistakes.fix: Restrict the second Remaining zone to a layer, or delete it.

protips: Leave Everything Else gentle. Gloss at intensity 50 is chosen to sit under sponsors and numbers without changing how they read.
A catch-all with Use source paint (spec only) is the cleanest way to change the shine of a whole livery without touching a colour.

articles.title: Zone card controls: mute, lock, reset, duplicate, delete
articles.summary: Use mute for a temporary comparison. Reset Zone clears material, drawn coverage and source-layer restrictions. Choice locks, layer paint locks and source-layer targeting are different controls. Linking copies selected finish properties, not every target or stack.
articles.what: The eye mutes a Zone while retaining its settings. Duplicate copies Zone settings and masks with a fresh identity; it does not duplicate imported artwork pixels. Reset Zone preserves its name but deletes the old properties and supplies defaults, including an empty region and no retained source-layer restriction. The chain icon uses an in-app target picker and copies its listed finish fields from the chosen target into the clicked Zone. Geometric coverage, source-layer restrictions and modern stacks are not in that copy list. BASE choice and colour locks have narrower meanings than a whole-project freeze. deep.heading: Different locks and their limits
deep.body: The padlock on the BASE row sets lockBase: it protects the base field during Randomize and also makes the inspected bulk-apply-finish path skip that zone. It is not a whole-zone freeze. Both Rand Current Zone and Rand All Zones clear the special finish field. Rand Current Zone also clears the pattern stack even when base or pattern is locked; the inspected Rand All Zones function retains the existing stack. Separate pattern and intensity locks govern their respective choices. Lock Base Color beside BASE COLOR sets lockBaseColor: it preserves the current colour/tint setup when picking a different material instead of filling the new defaults. It does not disable paint patterns or every later colour operation. It also does not make Use finish’s own color equivalent to Use source paint. Source mode is the separate control for skipping the reviewed ordinary primary-base paint function. Layer paint locks and layer-zone targeting locks belong to different controls; inspect their labels before choosing a lock.

deep.heading: Every icon on a card, and what it really does
deep.body: The eye mutes the zone: it is left out of the preview and the render, but kept. The overlapping-squares icon duplicates. The chain icon links two zones. The x deletes. The three-line handle drags to reorder. The padlock next to the BASE row only protects the base from the randomise buttons. There is no up and down arrow on the card any more; use the handle or Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down.

deep.heading: Delete asks first, and has limits
deep.body: If the zone has a finish, a colour or a drawn area, you get a question naming what would be lost. The last remaining zone cannot be deleted. After a delete, Ctrl+Z brings it back. Pressing Delete alone is reserved for pixel selections and shows a hint; Shift+Delete removes the selected zone.

deep.heading: Randomise is bolder than it looks
deep.body: Rand Current Zone, Rand All Zones and Shift+R pick a new base and pattern and a new intensity from 10 to 100 percent. They also clear the zone's special finish even when the base is locked. Rand Current Zone and Shift+R clear the zone's stack of extra patterns as well; Rand All Zones leaves each zone's pattern stack alone. With Smart Randomize ticked, which is the default, 8 times in 10 the pick comes from a list of combinations known to look good, and the rest avoids known bad ones. If either lock is on, smart mode steps aside.

deep.heading: Reset and linking scope
deep.body: The eye mutes a Zone while retaining its settings. Duplicate copies Zone settings and masks with a fresh identity; it does not duplicate imported artwork pixels. Reset Zone preserves its name but deletes the old properties and supplies defaults, including an empty region and no retained source-layer restriction. The chain icon uses an in-app target picker and copies its listed finish fields from the chosen target into the clicked Zone. Geometric coverage, source-layer restrictions and modern stacks are not in that copy list. BASE choice and colour locks have narrower meanings than a whole-project freeze. Check the actual target and control label before changing anything.

deep.heading: Duplicate is not new artwork
deep.body: duplicateZone requests a new Zone ID and cloned region/spatial/strength masks. It inserts the copy below the source; separate artwork-layer pixels are not created by this operation.

faq.q: How do I try different materials without resetting my colour setup?
faq.a: Enable Lock Base Color beside BASE COLOR before swapping the material. It preserves the current colour/tint setup during a finish pick. The BASE-row padlock is different: it protects the base from Randomize and the inspected bulk finish operation.

faq.q: Will locking Base Color disable paint patterns?
faq.a: No. Lock Base Color preserves the current colour setup when swapping a material; it does not disable paint patterns or freeze all exported pixels.

faq.q: Does locking the base keep my special finish and pattern stack during Randomize?
faq.a: The base field is protected, but both Rand Current Zone and Rand All Zones clear the special finish. Rand Current Zone also clears the pattern stack; the inspected Rand All Zones function retains it. This lock is not a whole-design freeze.

faq.q: What is the difference between the BASE padlock and Lock Base Color?
faq.a: The BASE-row padlock protects the base field from Randomize and skips that zone in the inspected bulk finish application. Lock Base Color preserves colour/tint setup when choosing another material. Neither is a whole-project pixel lock.

faq.q: Does Lock Base Color make a colour-bearing finish spec only?
faq.a: Not by itself. Choose Use source paint (spec only) to skip the reviewed ordinary primary base paint function. Lock Base Color keeps the existing colour setup on a material swap; the mode it keeps might be source, solid, finish colour or another choice.

faq.q: Why did a bulk finish operation skip my zone?
faq.a: The inspected bulk-apply-finish path skips zones whose BASE-row lockBase is on. Check that padlock before assuming the finish is unavailable.

faq.q: Does muting a zone delete it?
faq.a: No. A muted zone keeps every setting and is only skipped in the preview and render. The card shows Muted (excluded from render).

faq.q: I deleted a zone by accident. Can I get it back?
faq.a: Yes, press Ctrl+Z straight away. Deleted zones are on the undo list.

faq.q: What does Apply Finish to All do?
faq.a: After you confirm, it copies the selected zone's base, pattern, finish, intensity, scale and pattern stack to every other zone. Colours and drawn areas are not copied.

faq.q: Why did my chrome finish vanish after I randomised?
faq.a: Randomise clears a zone's special finish even if the base is locked. Undo with Ctrl+Z to get it back.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two locks?
faq.a: The padlock on the BASE row protects the base from randomise. The Lock checkbox beside Base Color keeps your colour when you change the finish, so you can swap a base purely for its shine.

faq.q: I locked the base before randomising one zone, but a pattern disappeared. What does the lock actually protect?
faq.a: The BASE choice lock does not freeze the whole design. The reviewed Randomize Current path clears the pattern stack even when the base/pattern is locked; Randomize All retains the existing stack. Both clear the special-finish field. Inspect which Randomize command was used and the history before restoring intended contributors.

mistakes.symptom: You locked the base but the finish still changed
mistakes.cause: The lock protects only the base material. A special finish is cleared by every randomise, and the pattern stack by Rand Current Zone and Shift+R.
mistakes.fix: Undo with Ctrl+Z, then pick the look again by hand. Do not randomise zones that use a special finish.

mistakes.symptom: Shift+Delete or Delete does nothing
mistakes.cause: Delete alone is reserved for pixel selections, and a text box may have focus.
mistakes.fix: Click the zone card, then press Shift+Delete, or use the x on the card.

mistakes.symptom: All your zones vanished and the list is back to the starting five
mistakes.cause: Reset All Zones replaces the whole list with Zone 1 to 4 plus Everything Else.
mistakes.fix: Press Ctrl+Z straight away. The confirm box warns you first, so read it before pressing OK.

protips: Reset Zone returns one zone to factory settings, while Reset All Zones returns the whole list to the starting five. Both can be undone.
Zone undo remembers the last 15 steps, so after a long shuffle or a few deletes the earliest changes can no longer be undone. Save a template before big experiments.
Randomise with Smart Randomize on is a fast way to audition combinations. Undo is one keypress, so try ten before you decide.

articles.title: Add a zone and pick a colour from the car
articles.summary: The fastest way to make a zone: add it, press PICK COLOR FROM CAR, and click the colour you want on the paint.
articles.what: PICK COLOR FROM CAR arms an eyedropper. Click a colour on the canvas and the zone grabs every pixel of that colour. Each further click adds another colour. You can also type a hex colour and press Apply, or use the colour wheel, which applies live. Typing a hex colour chooses which paint pixels to catch; it does not recolour them. To recolour, use BASE > Base Color > Use solid color. The Color tool in the toolbar (I) does the same job with extra buttons: + Add Color, Set and Exclude.
when: You want a finish on "the red stripe" or "the green body".
You know the exact colour of the area.
how: 1. Press + Add Zone, then click the new card.
2. In COLOR press PICK COLOR FROM CAR.
3. Click the colour on the canvas. Click again to add shades.
4. If edges are left over, slide Color Match toward Loose.
5. In BASE, pick a finish.

deep.heading: Every click lands in the selected zone
deep.body: A pick always goes into the zone whose card is highlighted at that moment, even if you launched the picker from another zone. Check the selected card before you click. Each pick becomes a colour chip showing its hex code, a small Exact to Loose slider and a red x to remove it. The toast tells you how many colours are now stacked, for example Added #C8102E to Zone 1 (2 colors stacked).

deep.heading: New chips copy the zone's tolerance
deep.body: A fresh chip starts at the zone's own tolerance: plus or minus 40 for Zone 1, Zone 2 and Everything Else, 35 for Zone 3 and 30 for Zone 4. The same colour cannot be added twice. If you pick one the zone already has, you get a message that it is already there and no new chip appears. Remove a chip with its x, which can be undone.

deep.heading: Hex box, wheel and Apply
deep.body: Type six hex digits, with or without the hash, then press Apply. A wrong code shows Enter a valid hex code like #FF3366. In a zone that already has several colours, Apply adds another chip. In a zone with none, it sets one. The colour wheel applies live as you drag. Either way this chooses which pixels are caught. It never recolours them.

deep.heading: To actually change the colour
deep.body: Open BASE and set Base Color to Use solid color, then choose a colour or type a hex. Or pick a finish that brings its own colour. Colour match decides where; Base Color decides what comes out. Mixing these two up is the most common colour mistake.

deep.heading: What the click reads
deep.body: The picker reads the colour of your source paint under the cursor, not the finished preview. Hide the zone overlay if it covers the colour you want, so you can see what you are picking. Edge pixels are blends of two colours, so click the middle of a flat area.

The same pick can come from the Color tool in the toolbar, which adds Set, + Add Color and Exclude buttons.
When a colour also appears where it should not, Exclude paints those places out of the match.

faq.q: Does typing a hex colour recolour my paint?
faq.a: No. It only chooses which pixels belong to the zone. To recolour, set BASE > Base Color to Use solid color.

faq.q: How many colours can one zone hold?
faq.a: As many as you need. Each pick adds a chip. Keep the list short so the zone stays easy to read.

faq.q: Why did my click not add a colour?
faq.a: That exact colour is already in the zone, or no paint is loaded yet. You will see a message saying so.

faq.q: Can I take back a pick?
faq.a: Yes. Press Ctrl+Z, or click the red x on that colour chip. Both are undoable.

faq.q: Which zone does the click go to?
faq.a: The one currently selected on the left. Click a card first, then pick.

faq.q: How do I add a zone?
faq.a: Press + Add Zone, click the new card, press PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click the colour you want on the paint (or pick a part), then choose a finish in BASE. A zone is a group of pixels that gets one finish.

faq.q: How do I recolour only the red parts to blue?
faq.a: Pick the red as a zone: + Add Zone, PICK COLOR FROM CAR and click the red on the paint, raise the tolerance if edges are left over, then set BASE > Base Color to Use solid color and choose blue. Picking a colour only chooses the pixels; the Base Color sets what they become.

mistakes.symptom: The colour went into the wrong zone
mistakes.cause: A different card was selected when you clicked the canvas.
mistakes.fix: Undo, select the correct zone card, and pick again. The selected card is always the target.

mistakes.cause: Shaded and anti-aliased pixels sit outside the plus or minus 40 reach of one shade.
mistakes.fix: Click a second, darker shade on the same stripe, or slide the chip toward Loose.

mistakes.symptom: Typed a hex and the colour on the car did not change
mistakes.cause: The hex box selects pixels. It does not apply colour.
mistakes.fix: Open BASE and choose Use solid color to paint a new colour.

protips: Click near the middle of a flat area. Edge pixels are blends of two colours and make a poor starting point.
Pick a colour on a layer and the app warns you if that colour sits outside the zone's layer restriction, naming the layer it really lives on.

articles.title: Colour tolerance and refining a colour
articles.summary: Colour tolerance controls how close a pixel must be to the picked colour. It does not identify numbers, sponsors or body panels: identical colours elsewhere can match too. Use a checked layer restriction or local region/mask to isolate artwork. In the inspected layer-RGB fast path a selector tolerance0 falls back to30, so zero is not proof of exact-match-only coverage. Other selection paths must be checked separately.
articles.what: The tolerance slider runs from 0 (Exact) to 100 (Loose) and shows the value as plus or minus a number. Around 30 to 50 is normal and 6 is about the exact shade only. Zone 1 and Zone 2 start at 40, Zone 3 at 35, Zone 4 at 30, and zones you add start at 40. Do not leave it at 0: a value of 0 is read as 40 when the preview and render are built. Raise it when the edges of an area look chewed or lettering has a fringe. Lower it when neighbouring colours get caught. Hard Edge cuts the zone edge sharp instead of softly anti-aliased, which suits crisp lettering and thin lines. Refine color keeps the colour selection but lets you paint a green brush to limit it to places you choose.
when: The edges of the selected area look rough.
Neighbouring colours get caught in the zone.
how: 1. Select the zone and find the tolerance slider next to its colour chip.
2. Drag it up if you see leftover fringe, down if too much is caught.
3. Turn on Hard Edge for crisp lettering.
4. Use Refine color to paint away the places where the colour should not apply.

controls.label: Color Match (the Exact to Loose slider on each picked colour chip)
controls.range: 0-100 on each picked colour chip (0 = exact shade only); default 40
controls.effect: How many nearby shades of the picked colour the zone grabs. Slide toward Exact for only that shade, toward Loose for lighter, darker and similar shades too (about 30-50 is normal). Every picked colour chip has its own slider; there is no zone-wide one.

controls.label: Hard Edge
controls.effect: Cuts the zone edge sharp instead of softly anti-aliased.

controls.label: Refine color
controls.effect: Keeps the colour selection but lets you paint a green brush to limit it to places you choose.

tips: Watch the overlay on the canvas while you drag the slider.
To select by finish instead of by colour, use Select > Material, which has its own tolerance and soft edge.
pitfalls: A tolerance of 0 does not mean exact: it is treated as 40.
Hard edges can look jagged on diagonal lines.
Refine color needs a colour already set on the zone.
Zero tolerance is replaced by 40 in the inspected common render payload.
Identical colours in different places are not separated by colour tolerance.
A whole-image colour pick is not a number or sponsor identity detector.

deep.heading: One slider per colour, not per zone
deep.body: Each colour chip has its own slider running from Exact on the left to Loose on the right, with a plus or minus number beside it from 0 to 100. The old single slider for the whole zone is gone. New chips start at the zone's setting, which is 40 for most zones. The helper line under the chips explains it: Exact grabs only that colour, Loose also grabs its nearby shades such as shadows, highlights and gradients.

deep.heading: What the number measures
deep.body: The number is a distance on a 0 to 255 scale, but colours are not weighed equally: green counts most (0.59), red next (0.30) and blue least (0.11). At plus or minus 40 a pixel can differ from your pick by up to about 52 levels in pure green, 73 in pure red or 121 in pure blue. So a wide blue shift is forgiven long before a green one. At 12 those limits are 16, 22 and 36.

deep.heading: A ramp, not a switch
deep.body: A pixel exactly on your colour is caught at full strength, and strength falls in a straight line to zero at the tolerance. Hard Edge, which is on by default in every zone, then turns any pixel with a trace of strength into a fully owned pixel, so the edge is crisp. With Hard Edge off, pixels below about 15 percent strength are softened instead, which blends the zone's edge into its neighbours.

deep.heading: Zero does not mean exact
deep.body: A tolerance of 0 is treated as the default of 40 when the picture is built, because an empty value falls back to 40. For a truly tight match use 5. The slider shows what you set, but the render uses 40 at 0, so do not rely on the far left end.

deep.heading: Refine color for what tolerance cannot fix
deep.body: Tolerance is about colour only. When two areas share one colour, narrowing the slider will not separate them. Use Refine color, which lets you paint a green brush over the places the colour should apply, or add a layer or area limit.

Exclude paints away places a loose match caught by mistake.
A layer limit lets you use a tight match on the right art without bleeding into other art.

faq.q: What number should I use?
faq.a: About 30 to 50 for big flat colours. 10 to 16 for dark fills next to black strokes. Start at the default 40 and adjust while watching the overlay.

faq.q: Is it the same slider for the whole zone?
faq.a: No. Each colour chip has its own. A zone with two colours has two sliders.

faq.q: Why does a bright blue grab more than a bright red at the same number?
faq.a: Blue differences count least in the match, so a larger blue shift still fits inside the same number.

faq.q: What does Hard Edge do to tolerance?
faq.a: Nothing to the reach. It makes the edge crisp: any pixel inside the reach becomes fully owned instead of fading.

faq.q: I set the slider to 0 and the zone still catches a lot.
faq.a: Zero falls back to 40 in the render. Use 5 for the tightest real setting.

faq.q: Weird glowing line across the car where two colours meet
faq.a: That glow is an edge halo from the zone edge: lower the Colour tolerance for the colour beside it (10 to 16 for dark fills next to black strokes), or use Refine selection (shrink, feather or smooth) to adjust the zone edge. Check the preview after each change.

faq.q: Will a colour tolerance of zero separate white logos from a white body?
faq.a: No. Colour matching cannot tell identical colours apart by their location or purpose. In the inspected common render payload, a zero tolerance is replaced by 40, so zero is not a reliable exact-match setting there. Use a checked local mask or genuinely separate artwork to isolate the logos.

faq.q: Why did picking the number colour also select the body?
faq.a: Colour matching can include the same colour anywhere in the allowed target. Lowering tolerance excludes different colours, but cannot separate identical number and body pixels. Add a checked layer restriction or local region/mask.

faq.q: Can tightening tolerance protect sponsors that share the body colour?
faq.a: Not by itself. Identical colours still match. Protect the sponsor area with genuinely separate artwork or a checked local region/mask, and inspect the coverage before choosing a material.

faq.q: How do I isolate numbers on a flat paint when their colour is repeated elsewhere?
faq.a: A flat image has no separate semantic number layer. Use a checked local selection or mask around the actual number artwork, or separate the artwork first. A colour pick can help build a candidate selection, but does not prove that only numbers are included.

mistakes.symptom: Sponsor text looks chewed or has coloured fringes
mistakes.cause: The tolerance is too tight for anti-aliased edge pixels.
mistakes.fix: Move that chip toward Loose in steps of about 10 until the fringe is covered, with Hard Edge left on.

mistakes.symptom: A zone leaks onto the neighbouring colour
mistakes.cause: The tolerance is too loose, or the two colours are close in green.
mistakes.fix: Lower the slider and watch the overlay. Green differences count most, so similar greens need the tightest settings.

mistakes.symptom: Exact at 0 behaves like 40
mistakes.cause: A zero tolerance is replaced by the default when the picture is built.
mistakes.fix: Use 5 for an almost exact match.

protips: Green carries more weight than blue, so two blues that look different may still be inside one tolerance while two close greens may not be.
Watch the overlay on the canvas while you drag the slider. The edge of the selection moves with it, so you can stop the moment the fringe is covered.

articles.title: Draw box, lasso and region: limiting a zone to an area
articles.summary: APPLY AREA limits a zone to a drawn box or lasso shape, on top of its colour or layer choice. Use it for "only the hood" or "only the bottom half".
articles.what: Draw box lets you click and drag a rectangle on the paint; the zone only affects what is inside. Lasso draws a free-hand outline for areas that are not rectangles; close it by returning near the start. Both are on the flat unwrapped sheet, so one box may cover several car panels. Clear removes the area, Activate turns a stored area back on, and Refine color paints a brush mask inside the colour selection. You can also give a zone the selection you made with the Rect, Lasso or Wand tools by pressing Use Region.
when: A colour appears in more than one place and you want only one.
You want a finish on a single panel.
how: Select the intended Zone and open APPLY AREA. Choose Draw box for a rectangle or Lasso for a traced footprint on the Source canvas.
Drag the rectangle or close the lasso around the verified artwork area. Sheet coordinates are not calibrated physical-car panel coordinates.
Inspect the coverage overlay together with the Zone's colour and layer restrictions. A drawn footprint can still be limited to picked colours or restricted layers.
Use Clear if the footprint is wrong, then check coverage again. This edits Zone coverage, not the editable layer pixels.

deep.heading: A drawn area is an extra filter, not a replacement
deep.body: The box or lasso is multiplied with the zone's colour match, so the zone covers only pixels that pass both: the colour, and inside the shape. If the zone has no colour at all, the shape alone is the zone. That makes a box with a colour the easiest way to say red hood, not the red stripe on the side.

deep.heading: Include and Exclude brushes sit on top
deep.body: After the shape and the colour, the green Include and red Exclude brushes are applied. Anything painted red is removed. If you painted any green at all, the zone is limited to the green areas only. So one stroke of green can shrink a zone to a small patch, which surprises people who meant to add to it.

deep.heading: Drawing the shapes
deep.body: For a box, drag it out. Shift makes a square, Alt grows it from the centre and Esc cancels. For a lasso, drag freehand and let go to close it, or click polygon points and finish with a double-click or Enter. Backspace removes the last point. Clicking near the first point also closes it. A lasso needs at least 3 points or you get a message asking for a wider loop.

deep.heading: Nudge instead of redrawing
deep.body: Pick the Move Selection Border tool in the toolbar. Then an arrow key moves the zone's drawn area 1 pixel, and Shift plus an arrow key moves it 10 pixels. You can also drag inside it. Only the border moves; the paint pixels stay where they are. This is how you line up a box edge to a panel edge without starting over.

deep.heading: What copies and what does not
deep.body: Duplicating a zone copies its drawn area. Saving a template does not: templates keep finishes, colours, tolerances, pattern, intensity, scale and locks, but not boxes, lassos or layer limits. After loading a template, redraw the areas.

combos.why: Naming a part gives an exact mask of the panel, which is cleaner than a box when the car is known.
Use Region hands a selection to a zone, and Exclude trims it afterwards.
The Rect and Lasso tools make the same shapes and Use Region gives them to a zone.

faq.q: Is a box one rectangle on the car?
faq.a: It is one rectangle on the flat sheet. The hood and roof are separate islands, so one box can cover parts of both.

faq.q: How do I remove a box?
faq.a: Press Clear in APPLY AREA. Activate turns a stored area back on.

faq.q: Can I save a box in a template?
faq.a: No. Templates keep finishes and colours, not drawn areas or layer limits.

faq.q: My lasso did nothing.
faq.a: It needs 3 or more points, and a freehand loop must be wide enough. The app tells you which.

faq.q: Does a box cut through the colour or add to it?
faq.a: It cuts. Colour and shape both must match, so a box can only make the zone smaller.

mistakes.symptom: The zone covers a stray rectangle you forgot about
mistakes.cause: An old box is still stored on the zone.
mistakes.fix: Open APPLY AREA and press Clear.

mistakes.symptom: Paint with the green brush and most of the zone vanished
mistakes.cause: Once any green is painted, the zone is limited to green areas only.
mistakes.fix: Undo, or Clear the area and paint Exclude in red for places you want removed instead.

mistakes.symptom: After loading a template, the hood zone covers the whole car
mistakes.cause: Templates do not store drawn areas, so the box is gone and only the colour rule is left.
mistakes.fix: Open APPLY AREA on that zone and draw the box again, or tie it to a layer.

protips: Combine a box with a colour for precision: red plus the hood box catches only the hood's red.
Use the Move Selection Border tool, not undo and redraw, to line an edge up to a panel edge. One arrow press is exactly 1 pixel on the 2048 sheet.

articles.title: Exclude, Set and Use Region
articles.summary: Exclude, Set and Use Region are the Color tool's buttons for fine-tuning what a zone catches.
articles.what: With the Color tool active, a small bar appears. + Add Color adds the clicked colour to the chosen zone. Set replaces the zone's colour with just this one colour. Exclude removes areas from the zone's colour match, shown red on the canvas. Use Region gives the zone the shape you just selected (box, lasso or brush) instead of a colour. On the selection bar, Include paints areas to keep (green) and Exclude paints areas to remove (red).
when: A zone catches a spot you do not want.
You want to select by shape instead of by colour.
how: 1. Pick the Color tool (I) and choose the zone from the dropdown in its bar.
2. Click + Add Color to add a shade, or Set to start over with one colour.
3. Press Exclude, then paint over the places to remove.
4. Or make a selection with Rect or Lasso and press Use Region.

tips: Red on the canvas means removed, green means kept.
pitfalls: Set replaces the zone's colours. Use + Add Color to keep the old ones.
aliases: remove an area from a zone

deep.heading: Four buttons, four different jobs
deep.body: + Add Color stacks the colour you last clicked into the chosen zone as one more chip. Set throws away every chip and makes that one colour the zone's only colour. Exclude switches to a red brush that removes places from the colour match. Use Region gives the zone your current Rect, Lasso, Brush or Wand selection with no colour needed. The small zone box beside them chooses which zone receives the colour.

deep.heading: Exclude removes, Include limits
deep.body: Red from Exclude is subtracted from the zone. Green from Include works the other way: once any green exists, the zone is limited to the green. The two brushes are applied after the colour and any drawn shape, so they refine without replacing anything. Both are saved with the zone and are copied when you duplicate it.

deep.heading: What Set really does
deep.body: Set puts the zone into single-colour mode using the zone's own tolerance, usually 40, and clears the stack. The toast says set to the hex code (single color). In single-colour mode the zone may not show its own Color Match slider. If you miss it, click the same colour and press + Add Color: the app answers that the colour is ready and the Color Match controls are restored.

deep.heading: Use Region and its fallbacks
deep.body: Use Region sends the selection to the zone selected on the left. If that zone has no selection yet, it uses the first zone that has one. If no zone has a selection, it tells you to draw a region first with Rect, Lasso, Brush or Wand. On success the toast reports how many pixels and what percent of the sheet the region covers.

examples.result: The zone has only that colour. Earlier chips are gone.

examples.title: Zone from a drawn shape with no colour
examples.goal: Give a freehand patch its own finish.
examples.result: The toast shows the pixel count and percent. Now choose a Base Material for the zone.

combos.why: + Add Color from the Color tool does the same stacking as PICK COLOR FROM CAR.
Use Region and the drawn box share one stored area on the zone.
Refine tools shape a selection before you hand it over with Use Region.

faq.q: What is the difference between Set and + Add Color?
faq.a: Set replaces everything with one colour. + Add Color keeps the old colours and adds one more.

faq.q: Red or green on the canvas, which is which?
faq.a: Red is removed from the zone. Green is kept. The selection bar buttons Include and Exclude paint those.

faq.q: Does Use Region need a colour?
faq.a: No. A zone can be only a region.

faq.q: Can I undo an Exclude stroke?
faq.a: Yes, with Ctrl+Z. Set and Use Region are undoable too.

faq.q: Why does Use Region say draw a region first?
faq.a: No zone has a stored selection yet. Draw one with Rect, Lasso, Brush or Wand, then press it again.

mistakes.symptom: Pressing Set wiped a carefully built colour list
mistakes.cause: Set replaces the stack with one colour by design.
mistakes.fix: Undo with Ctrl+Z, and use + Add Color to add shades without losing the old ones.

mistakes.symptom: One stroke of green shrank the zone to a patch
mistakes.cause: Include limits the zone to the green areas once any exist.
mistakes.fix: Undo, or use Exclude to remove places instead of Include.

mistakes.symptom: Use Region applied to the wrong zone
mistakes.cause: The zone highlighted on the left was not the one you meant.
mistakes.fix: Undo, click the right zone card, and press Use Region again.

protips: The toast after Use Region tells you how many pixels and what percent of the sheet you gave the zone. A tiny percent means a tiny shape.
Use Region needs no colour, so a hand-drawn patch can carry its own finish without any colour match at all.

articles.title: Restricting a zone to layers
articles.summary: RESTRICT TO LAYERS limits a zone to the selected layers' visible ownership. Inspect actual layer contents and the resulting coverage; layer names alone do not identify body paint, numbers or sponsors.
articles.what: With suitable layered artwork, tick one or more actual layers under RESTRICT TO LAYERS. The inspected ownership path uses the rendered source footprint at alpha 128 or greater and excludes above-art footprints at alpha 128 or greater. The compositor includes opacity, clipping, visibility and visible effects; blend is normalized for ownership rather than used as a colour cue. Multiple selected layers contribute the union of their visible ownership. Empty or hidden contributions cannot be assumed to cover the car. Clearing the selected restrictions removes this limit and can broaden the zone. A layer restriction is not automatic semantic recognition and is not a complete copy of Photoshop clipping masks.
when: "Make the numbers chrome."
You want the body finish without touching sponsors.
how: Inspect the actual layered artwork and identify the intended visible target.
Select the zone and tick the actual artwork under RESTRICT TO LAYERS, or use MAKE ZONE on the suitable layer card.
Check zone coverage, including shared artwork, opacity and artwork above the target.
Choose the material and source-paint mode separately; keep protected artwork outside the material target where needed.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS (checkboxes per PSD layer)
controls.range: see SCHEMA: part names come from get_car_map; band 0-1 fractions (height = roof-line to rocker, length = front to rear); rect/cells only for details under ~12% of the sheet
controls.effect: Tick a layer (Car Paint, Sponsors, Numbers, Tape ...) and the zone only covers pixels that exist on that layer.

controls.label: Create a zone restricted to this layer
controls.effect: One click makes a zone that only covers this layer's pixels; then give it a finish.

controls.label: Lock the active zone to this layer (Ctrl+L)
controls.effect: Restricts the currently selected zone to this layer.

tips: Inspect the coverage before changing a material.
Keep separate material targets for the body and protected numbers/sponsors when their shine should differ.
pitfalls: A shared layer is not a body-only target.
A flattened image has no semantic sponsor or number layers.
Binary ownership is not a universal no-halo guarantee.
aliases: make a zone only affect one layer
clip a zone to a layer

deep.heading: Targets before materials
deep.body: A body zone and a sponsor zone need different targets if their material responses should differ. Inspect shared artwork and overlap: a layer name is only a label, and a body layer may also contain sponsor pixels.

deep.heading: Binary footprint boundary
deep.body: The inspected source mask uses source alpha >=128 and above alpha <128. This is a hard ownership decision at roughly half opacity; it does not guarantee perfectly soft edges or every final appearance.

combos.why: Use the actual layer target to restrict an existing zone; inspect what that layer contains.
Pixels without a zone owner can fall to the remainder; inspect the composed result.

faq.q: Can I tick more than one layer?
faq.a: Yes. The inspected helper takes the union of the selected layers' visible ownership. It does not assign different materials to those layers within one zone.

faq.q: What if my art has soft edges?
faq.a: The inspected mask uses source alpha >=128 and above-art alpha <128, making a binary ownership decision. Do not promise a smooth fractional blend at that boundary; inspect the actual coverage and output.

faq.q: Why does my layer zone paint nothing?
faq.a: Check missing layer IDs, layer or parent visibility, opacity, clipping and art covering it. The inspected payload sends an empty mask when a restricted target has no contribution; it does not silently grant whole-car coverage.

faq.q: Can layer names guarantee that my sponsors are protected?
faq.a: No. Inspect the actual layer contents and visible ownership. Artwork sharing a body layer may still be included. Use separate artwork or a checked local mask where necessary.

faq.q: Does clearing layer restrictions protect my artwork?
faq.a: No. Clearing removes that restriction and may broaden the zone. Check the remaining colour, region and spatial targeting before treating it as a body-only change.

faq.q: My logo and body are flattened together. Does restricting to the body layer protect it?
faq.a: Layer restriction alone cannot separate body and logo pixels on the same flattened layer. Use a checked spatial selection/mask that excludes the logo, or separate the artwork first. Inspect actual coverage and output; the layer name is not proof.

mistakes.symptom: A restricted zone covers nothing
mistakes.cause: Selected artwork may be hidden, missing, clipped, covered, or below the binary alpha threshold
mistakes.fix: Inspect actual layer IDs, visibility, opacity and ownership before changing artwork. Clearing restrictions can broaden the zone.

mistakes.symptom: A body material affects sponsor artwork
mistakes.cause: The selected layer or zone region includes both body and sponsor pixels
mistakes.fix: Use genuinely separate artwork or a checked local mask for different material targets.

mistakes.symptom: Visible guides prevent body coverage underneath
mistakes.cause: The inspected ownership helper includes visible above-art footprints and does not exclude them by layer name
mistakes.fix: Inspect the actual stack and intended guide visibility. Do not assume a layer called Mask or Wire is ignored.

articles.title: Named car parts: left side, hood, roof and more
articles.summary: Named-part placement requires a verified live map matching the loaded template. Unknown or unrecognized template geometry cannot promise precise logo placement on a hood or side; reference facts are not a UV map.
articles.what: Parts such as the hood, roof or sides can be targeted only when the current connection has a verified live map matching the loaded template. A catalogue entry, downloaded PSD, remembered name or one naming tap does not certify exact panel bounds or direction. For unknown or unrecognized geometry, explain the limitation and use the current app's supported calibration workflow. Do not invent UV coordinates or reuse a sibling model's layout. Verified parts may have portions or bands only when their bounds and direction are supported by that map.
when: You say "make the hood matte" in Chat.
Shokker asks you to show it the parts of your car.
how: Read the recognized template and verified live map for the current source.
If the named part, bounds or direction are unsupported, use the app's supported calibration workflow before placing artwork; do not guess.
For an authorized edit on a verified target, use supported tools and check the actual measured scope and preview.
tips: Parts names also work as "driver side" for left and "passenger side" for right.
pitfalls: Reference facts and inspected PSD metadata are not calibrated UV geometry.
A remembered map must match the loaded template; do not substitute a sibling vehicle.
Left and right are about the car, not the sheet. Verify panel direction before using a portion.

deep.heading: Reference identity and exact placement are different
deep.body: A reference can identify the car, official template and recorded source facts. It does not certify the loaded file, compatibility or UV placement. Use a verified live map and current capabilities before applying a named-part edit.

deep.heading: Unknown geometry
deep.body: Unknown or unrecognized panels need the current app's supported calibration workflow. A single name, picture or a map belonging to a sibling vehicle is not proof of exact panel bounds and direction.

examples.goal: Explain whether precise hood placement is possible.
examples.result: Explain the missing geometry and calibrate before placing; no guessed edit is made.

combos.why: Teaching parts is how an unknown car gets names. It is asked once per layout.
In plain Pro you draw the same areas with a box or lasso. Named parts are the exact version for Chat.
The car library and your teaching feed the same memory that Chat and the AI copilot use.

faq.q: Can a car reference tell me exactly where its hood is on an unrecognized template?
faq.a: No. Reference knowledge and PSD metadata do not certify UV geometry. A verified live map must match the loaded template; unknown geometry needs calibration before precise placement.

faq.q: Can I place a logo precisely on an unknown template?
faq.a: Only after the current app verifies the target map, panel bounds and direction for that loaded source. Do not infer them from another car or a remembered name.

faq.q: Can verified named parts have portions or bands?
faq.a: Yes, when the current map and connected tools support those bounds and directions. A rear-half or lower-door request must use that verified target.

faq.q: Is the left side the left of the flat sheet?
faq.a: No. It means the car's left side. Check the verified map and direction; an island may be flipped on the sheet.

mistakes.symptom: The stripe landed at the top of one side and the bottom of the other
mistakes.cause: A box was drawn on the flat sheet, and one side is upside down there.
mistakes.fix: Use named parts and a band from the roof-line, so each side is measured from its own roof-line.

mistakes.symptom: Chat keeps asking you to tap panels
mistakes.cause: Your car is not in the library and no layout was taught for it.
mistakes.fix: Tap each named panel once. The layout is remembered after that.

mistakes.symptom: A named zone covers the wrong panel
mistakes.cause: The wrong panel was tapped when teaching.
mistakes.fix: Teach that part again by tapping the correct panel.

protips: Say both sides at once. The same band is measured from each side's own roof-line, which is exactly what a flipped sheet needs.
Driver side, passenger side, bonnet and nose all work as everyday names, so you do not have to learn the official ones.

articles.title: The zone popout panel
articles.summary: The ZONE POPOUT PANEL is where one zone is edited. It floats beside the canvas and opens when you click a zone card.
articles.what: The panel has sections: COLOR (which pixels the zone owns), APPLY AREA (box or lasso), BASE (finish, colour source, strengths, scale, rotation and spec sliders), SPEC OVERLAYS, PATTERN and OVERLAYS (second to fifth base). A tab on the left of the canvas shows or hides the panel, and so does Shift+E. Reset Zone at the top returns that one zone to defaults.
when: You need to change a zone's colour, area or finish.
The zone controls vanished or are in the way.
how: 1. Click a zone card in the ZONES column. The panel opens.
2. Work down through COLOR, APPLY AREA and BASE.
3. To hide the panel, click the zone editor tab or press Shift+E. Press again to bring it back.

controls.range: see SCHEMA: part names come from get_car_map; band 0-1 fractions (height = roof-line to rocker, length = front to rear); rect/cells only for details under ~12% of the sheet
controls.effect: Decides WHICH PIXELS of the paint this zone owns: by clicked colour, by PSD layer, or as catch-all (Remaining).

controls.label: APPLY AREA (section)
controls.range: see SCHEMA: part names come from get_car_map; band 0-1 fractions (height = roof-line to rocker, length = front to rear); rect/cells only for details under ~12% of the sheet
controls.effect: Limits the zone to a drawn shape (box or lasso) or a refined colour area, on top of the colour/layer choice.

controls.effect: Everything about the surface look: finish, colour source, hue / saturation / brightness, strengths, scale, rotation, spec sliders.

tips: Collapse the left column too if you need the widest possible canvas.
pitfalls: The editor tab and Shift+E only toggle the panel. They do not change the zone.

deep.heading: The panel grows as you work
deep.body: With a brand-new zone the panel is short: COLOR, APPLY AREA and the Base Material button. The Hue Shift, Saturation, Brightness, Base Strength and Spec Strength sliders, the R Metal, G Rough and B Coat shifts, and the spec overlay stack only appear after you choose a Base Material or a finish. If a slider you expect is missing, pick a finish first.

deep.heading: What each section is for
deep.body: COLOR decides which pixels the zone owns. The RESTRICT TO LAYERS box appears at the top of COLOR only when a layered template is loaded. APPLY AREA limits it to a drawn shape. BASE holds the finish, Base Color, strengths and fine tuning. PATTERN adds a pattern on top with its own opacity, strength, scale and rotation. OVERLAYS is a stack of up to five base finishes blended over each other. Click a section header to fold it away.

deep.heading: Showing and hiding the panel
deep.body: The panel floats beside the canvas and opens on a zone click. Click the small zone editor tab on the left edge of the canvas to hide it, and again to bring it back. Shift+E does the same, but only while the panel is open. The tab tooltip says E, but a bare E is the eraser tool, so use Shift+E.

deep.heading: Edits are live and undoable
deep.body: Sliders update LIVE PREVIEW as you drag. Zone undo keeps the last 15 steps, with a dragged slider counted as one step. Reset Zone at the top returns just this zone to factory settings, and nothing else changes.

COLOR and APPLY AREA inside the panel are where every pixel rule lives.
The Hue Shift, Saturation and Brightness sliders in BASE are explained there.

faq.q: Where did my sliders go?
faq.a: They appear only after a Base Material or finish is chosen for the zone. Pick one in BASE.

faq.q: How do I hide the panel?
faq.a: Click the zone editor tab on the left of the canvas, or press Shift+E while the panel is open.

faq.q: Does hiding the panel change the zone?
faq.a: No. It only hides or shows the panel.

faq.q: What does Reset Zone reset?
faq.a: Only the open zone: its finish, colours, patterns and sliders. Reset All Zones in the left column resets every zone.

faq.q: Why is there no RESTRICT TO LAYERS box?
faq.a: It only shows when a layered template such as a PSD is loaded.

mistakes.symptom: Pressing E does not open the panel
mistakes.cause: A bare E is the eraser tool. The shortcut is Shift+E.
mistakes.fix: Use Shift+E, or click the zone editor tab on the left of the canvas.

mistakes.symptom: The panel is open but you cannot find Brightness
mistakes.cause: The zone has no Base Material yet, so the BASE sliders are not built.
mistakes.fix: Press Base Material and choose a finish.

mistakes.symptom: Shift+E does nothing
mistakes.cause: The panel has never been opened, because the shortcut only works while the panel is open.
mistakes.fix: Click a zone card first, then press Shift+E.

A messy zone does not need Reset All Zones: open that zone and press Reset Zone at the top of its panel. Every other zone keeps its settings.

articles.title: Zone presets and templates
articles.summary: Presets give you a ready-made zone layout, and templates save your own layout so you can reuse it on another paint.
articles.what: Presets Gallery (Zones > More) shows ready-made layouts; click one to load it. Each swatch shows the zone finishes. Save as Template stores your current zone layout under a name you choose, up to 60 characters; Load Template brings it back on another paint, and Shift+T opens the template library.
when: You want a quick starting look.
You have a layout you will use on several cars.
You want the same zone layout on several cars of a team.
how: 1. Open More above the zone list and press Presets Gallery. Click a preset.
2. To save your own, press Save as Template, type a name and press Save.
3. To reuse it, pick it from the Load Template dropdown on the new paint.

deep.heading: Three different libraries
deep.body: Presets Gallery holds 23 ready-made zone layouts in five groups: Show Car (4), Clean (2), Aggressive (6), Special Effect (6) and Themed (5). The Shokker Library, also opened with Shift+T, holds 12 livery templates such as Racing Stripe, Two-Tone Split, GT3 Livery and NASCAR Cup. Save as Template and the Load Template dropdown are your own saved layouts, kept on this computer.

deep.heading: Presets replace your zones at once
deep.body: Clicking a preset card swaps in its zones straight away, with no confirm box, and the toast reads Loaded preset. A preset leaves most colours empty on purpose: you click your own colours with the eyedropper afterwards. Only the quick colours are set, such as White for sponsors, Dark for dark areas and Remaining for the safety net. Save your own layout first if you want it back.

deep.heading: Livery templates ask before replacing
deep.body: Applying a livery template asks to confirm when your zones already hold a finish or colour, saying your current zones will be replaced. It can be undone with Ctrl+Z. The library header reminds you to paint region masks with the brush after loading, because templates bring finishes, not areas.

deep.heading: What your own template remembers
deep.body: A saved template keeps each zone's name, colour choices and tolerances, base, pattern, special finish, intensity, scale, locks and pattern stack. It does not keep drawn boxes, lassos, brush areas or layer limits. Names run up to 60 characters, and saving under the same name overwrites the old one. Loading a template can be undone.

deep.heading: A template is a layout, not a paint
deep.body: Because colour picks are stored, a template made on one car often fits another car with the same colours, but a different livery needs new picks. When none of the loaded zones has a finish, the toast adds that you should now assign finishes.

combos.why: The recipe shows how to build by hand the same plan that presets and templates give you in one click.
Presets Gallery, Save as Template, Shokker Library and Undo History all sit in the More menu.
A template is only zones. Save SHOKK also keeps your paint and finishes in one file.

faq.q: Can I undo a preset?
faq.a: A preset swaps in immediately and shows no confirm box. Save your zones as a template first if you may want them back.

faq.q: Where are my templates stored?
faq.a: On this computer, inside the app. They are not in your paint file and do not travel to another PC.

faq.q: Why did a loaded template cover the whole car?
faq.a: Templates do not store drawn areas. The zone kept its colour rule only. Draw its area again.

faq.q: What is the difference between a preset and a template?
faq.a: Presets are built-in layouts. Templates are either the 12 livery templates in the Shokker Library or your own saved ones.

faq.q: Is there a limit on the template name?
faq.a: 60 characters. Use a name you will recognise, like 3-colour layout.

mistakes.symptom: You clicked a preset and lost your zones
mistakes.cause: Presets replace the whole zone list immediately.

deep.heading: Why this order works
deep.body: Each zone gets first pick of the pixels it matches, then the next zone, and Everything Else takes what is left. So the narrowest rules go first: trim by colour or layer, then hood and roof by box, then the body colour, then Everything Else. Hood and roof must sit above the body zone. deep.heading: Box plus colour, or box alone
deep.body: A hood zone with a colour and a box catches only that colour inside the box, which keeps hood graphics and decals out of the finish. A hood zone with only a box covers everything on that island, graphics included. Pick colour plus box when the hood carries artwork you want left alone.

deep.heading: A shine ladder for the four zones

In the spec map the middle number is roughness, so a lower number means a smoother, brighter reflection, and clearcoat 16 is the maximum gloss. Use two or three steps apart, not neighbours, so zones read as different on the car.

deep.body: Numbers by layer need no colour. If you pick the fill, 10 to 16 keeps the outline out. Stripes and trim work at 25 to 35 because they are flat colours. Large body colours at 40 handle shading. Looser than 50 starts to grab neighbours.
